entries.test: Public adoption data showing whether personal AI agents become universal and companies deploy large numbers of them would test this forecast.
Public valuations and labor studies showing whether AI agents are worth trillions and perform a huge fraction of human knowledge work would test the firm forecast.
entries.note: Physical labor is only a possibility; the knowledge-work and valuation predictions are firm.

entries.test: Public deployment and labor data through 2027 would show whether agents performed a huge fraction of human knowledge work beyond narrow use cases.
entries.note: The complete forecast runs through the end of 2027.

entries.test: Documented production deployments during 2025 would establish whether AI agents progressed beyond demonstrations that year.
Independent repeated trials and documented failure rates for 2025 AI agent demos would establish their reliability.
entries.note: Reliability has a plain practical reading despite the absence of a numerical threshold.

entries.test: Public repeated tests of ChatGPT Tasks would show whether scheduled actions consistently execute correctly at the requested times.
entries.note: The surrounding paragraph identifies ChatGPT Tasks as the target; no explicit deadline is given.

entries.test: Public reports published after January 15 throughout the remainder of 2025 would show whether numerous further agent failures and brittleness reports appeared.
Public evaluations of agents whose underlying models still hallucinate would test whether reliable operation is possible without solving hallucination.
entries.note: This asserts a necessary technical condition that counterexamples could refute.

entries.test: Research and independently replicated evaluations available by January 15, 2025 would show whether a principled solution reliably addressed hallucination.
entries.note: The claim concerns the state of available solutions at publication.

entries.test: Public capability evaluations and system descriptions would test whether functioning agents can operate without the capacities Marcus identifies as necessary.
entries.note: The source specifies enough theory of mind to infer user intentions; the normalization drops that functional qualification.

entries.test: Public evaluations of agents built from generative AI alone would test whether they reliably achieve the common sense, reasoning, grounding, instruction-following and intention inference described.
entries.note: The source conditions its conclusion on the preceding capability requirements, including intention inference. The normalization substitutes “capable agents” and presents a causal explanation as an observation.

entries.test: Repeated public agent trials and prospective predictions of their outcomes would test whether prompts produce mixed successes and strange results that are difficult to anticipate.
entries.note: “Unpredictably” is stronger than “difficult to know in advance,” and the normalization loses the source's prompt-dependent qualification.
